content: When a recommendation is expected to have the greatest impact in a specific setting, a strong recommendation is deemed appropriate. If the recommendation is likely to enhance access to an intervention for those most in need, it is also likely to warrant a strong recommendation. The higher the acceptability of the recommendation among stakeholders, the greater the likelihood of a strong recommendation. These decisions are based on values, preferences, acceptability, resource implications, and the feasibility of implementing the intervention. During the meeting, the chairs and methodologists worked to achieve consensus. After discussing all comments and questions from the group members, the chair asked whether the members agreed with the recommendations to document consensus. Voting was not required, but the group had previously agreed that a two-thirds majority would be necessary for a decision. Ultimately, all group members agreed with the recommendations. For each recommendation, the group also evaluated implementation needs and identified areas requiring further research. Before finalization, the draft guidelines were reviewed and revised by the Guidelines Development Group and an external review group. In accordance with WHO policy, all external contributors, including members of the Guidelines Development Group and the External Review Group, completed a WHO declaration of interest form. This included information on consulting, advisory panel participation, research support, and financial investments. Before the guideline meeting, brief biographies of each Guidelines Development Group member were posted online. The WHO Steering Committee reviewed the declarations and assessed potential conflicts of interest, agreeing on an approach to manage them. At the meeting, declarations of interest were reported per WHO standards. Individuals or organizations receiving significant funding from private companies (primarily pharmaceutical) or researchers/clinicians receiving honoraria exceeding $5000 from pharmaceutical companies were considered to have a conflict of interest if it related to the guideline topic. Their participation was classified as restricted. For example, Jason Grebely's participation was restricted for the topic of point-of-care HCV RNA viral load assays. He contributed technical expertise in reviewing evidence summaries but was excluded from voting and formulating recommendations. Declarations of interest from the External Review Group were reviewed according to WHO policy, and no cases required exclusion from the review process. Any identified conflicts of interest were considered when interpreting comments from the External Review Group during the external review process. However, external reviewers could not and did not make changes to the recommendations. The updated guidelines will be disseminated electronically via the WHO HHS departmental website, WHO regional and country offices, and ministries of health through webinars. They will also be available as print publications on demand and as policy briefs. Dissemination will be further supported by publishing systematic reviews and evidence in peer-reviewed journals. Successful implementation of the recommendations will depend on a well-planned process of adaptation and integration into regional and national strategies. Implementation can be measured by the number of countries incorporating the guidelines into their national treatment programs and updated data on HCV viral load testing and treatment uptake. WHO monitors the number of HCV-infected adults, adolescents, and children treated. The guidelines will be updated based on regular scoping exercises of available evidence and country implementation experiences. As evidence or user needs change, technical updates on specific subjects may be considered. For the treatment of chronic hepatitis C infection, pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens are recommended for all adults, adolescents, and children aged three years and above, regardless of disease stage. Pangenotypic regimens are defined as achieving a sustained virological response (SVR) rate of >85% across all six major HCV genotypes. Strong recommendations with moderate certainty of evidence apply to adults (≥18 years), adolescents (12–17 years), and older children (6–11 years). For younger children (3–5 years), a conditional recommendation is made with very low certainty of evidence. The recommended pangenotypic DAA regimens include: Sofosbuvir/Daclatasvir (SOF/DCV) for 12 weeks: High certainty of evidence for adults, adolescents, and older children; very low certainty for younger children. Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) for 12 weeks: High certainty of evidence for adults; low certainty for adolescents and older children; very low certainty for younger children. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir (G/P) for eight weeks: High certainty of evidence for adults; moderate certainty for adolescents and older children; very low certainty for younger children. For those without cirrhosis, treatment duration is typically 12 weeks. For individuals with compensated cirrhosis or those who are treatment-experienced, a 24-week regimen is recommended. In settings with a high prevalence of genotype 3 (>10%), specific regimens may be considered. Non-pangenotypic regimens, such as Sofosbuvir/Ledipasvir (SOF/LDV), are recommended in settings with minimal genotype 3 infection. Short-course, oral, curative DAA regimens have revolutionized HCV treatment in adults due to their high efficacy and minimal side effects compared to interferon-based regimens. However, until recently, there was limited attention to HCV in children and adolescents, and no DAA regimens were approved for use in children. The predominant mode of HCV transmission in children is mother-to-child transmission, while older children and adolescents may acquire the infection through unsafe injections and poor infection control, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Most children with HCV infection are asymptomatic or have mild liver disease, with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma being rare. However, recent evidence suggests that perinatally exposed individuals may develop cirrhosis at an earlier age. Early diagnosis and treatment in children are crucial to preventing long-term morbidity. Since 2018, the high rates of HCV viral clearance observed in adults with pangenotypic DAA regimens have been replicated in adolescents and children, leading to regulatory approvals by the FDA and EMA. Among adolescents, pangenotypic regimens such as Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir, Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir, and Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir/Voxilaprevir were approved in 2020 and 2021. For children aged three years and older, Sofosbuvir/Ledipasvir was approved in 2019, followed by Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir and Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir in 2021. However, the Sofosbuvir/Daclatasvir regimen, widely available and low-cost in LMICs, lacks regulatory approval for children and adolescents due to the absence of collaboration between originator companies. Aligning WHO-recommended DAA regimens across all age groups would simplify procurement, promote access to treatment for children in LMICs, and support global elimination efforts. A WHO-commissioned systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of key DAA regimens in adolescents (12–18 years), older children (6–11 years), and younger children (3–5 years) with chronic HCV infection. The review included 49 studies (3 RCTs, 28 non-RCTs, and 18 observational studies) involving 1891 adolescents, 472 older children, and 167 younger children. Sustained virological response rates 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12) were high (≥95%) across all age groups and regimens. Adverse events were reported in 50% of adolescents, but serious adverse events were rare. Treatment discontinuation rates were low. The strength of evidence was high for Sofosbuvir/Daclatasvir, moderate for Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir and Sofosbuvir/Ledipasvir, and low for Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir.
